hypothesis: Leukotriene F4 (KEGG C06462; LMFA03020009) is increased or characteristic in 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants.
rationale: Multiple targeted searches for leukotriene F4 (LTF4) in the context of infant gut metabolome, stool/fecal metabolomics, feeding stage, weaning, or age-related change returned no study - human or animal - reporting this compound in relation to infant age or milk-versus-complementary feeding. All directly relevant hits for LTF4 itself were chemical/vendor catalogue and database entries (Santa Cruz, Cayman, MedChemExpress, GlpBio, HMDB0006465, FooDB), several of which explicitly note that LTF4 is a cysteinyl-leukotriene generated in vitro from LTE4 by gamma-glutamyl transferase and has not been reported in vivo - which itself argues against a robust, well-characterized in vivo signal in infant stool. What exists is only generic, pathway-level reasoning in the hypothesized direction: (i) human milk delivers arachidonic acid at relatively fixed, substantial levels plus preformed lipid mediators, including pro-inflammatory leukotriene B4, so a milk-dominant 5-month diet could plausibly supply more 5-LOX/cysteinyl-leukotriene pathway substrate and mediators to the gut lumen than a more solid-food, milk-diluted 12-month diet; (ii) fecal ARA-derived oxylipins are measurable in vivo and change with postnatal age in suckling piglets. Neither of these addresses LTF4 specifically, nor a 5- versus 12-month contrast in human infants. Broader infant fecal metabolome studies located (e.g. longitudinal profiling across 1, 6, 12, 18, 24 months; feeding-pattern metabolome studies at 1 and 6 months; preterm sepsis microbiome/metabolome work that reported a dihydro-hydroxy-leukotriene E4 species) demonstrate that leukotriene-pathway species can be detected in infant stool, but none reported LTF4 as higher at ~5-6 months than at 12 months. This is therefore weak/theoretical support only (score 1), not absent evidence (0) and not contradicting evidence (-1), since nothing reported the opposite direction for this feature+group combination either.

evidence.title: Arachidonic Acid in Human Milk
evidence.study_population: Review of human milk composition (lactating women / breastfed infants)
evidence.relevance: Indirect/background: documents that human milk supplies arachidonic acid, the precursor of leukotrienes, supporting a general rationale that eicosanoid-pathway substrate delivery is greater during milk-dominant early infancy than after transition to family foods; does not address LTF4 or a 5- vs 12-month comparison.

evidence.title: High levels of anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving lipid mediators lipoxins and resolvins and declining docosahexaenoic acid levels in human milk during the first month of lactation
evidence.study_population: Human milk samples from lactating mothers (first month of lactation)
evidence.relevance: Indirect: shows preformed lipoxygenase-pathway lipid mediators, including leukotriene B4, are present in human milk, supporting the theoretical possibility that milk-fed infants receive/excrete more leukotriene-pathway species; no data on LTF4 or infant age contrasts.

evidence.title: The Quantitative Profiling of Oxylipins from Arachidonic Acid by LC-MS/MS in Feces at Birth 3 Days and 21 Days of Piglets
evidence.study_population: Suckling piglets, fecal oxylipin profiling at postnatal days 3 and 21
evidence.relevance: Indirect animal evidence that arachidonic-acid-derived oxylipins are quantifiable in feces and vary with postnatal age; it is a neonatal suckling window (not 5 vs 12 months of human age) and does not report leukotriene F4.

evidence.title: Longitudinal development of the gut microbiome and metabolome in preterm neonates with late onset sepsis and healthy controls
evidence.study_population: Preterm human neonates (sepsis cases and healthy controls), longitudinal stool microbiome/metabolome
evidence.relevance: Establishes that cysteinyl-leukotriene-related species (a dihydro-hydroxy-leukotriene E4 metabolite) are detectable in infant stool and can vary with host/microbial state, but the reported variation relates to sepsis, not to infant age or complementary feeding, and LTF4 itself is not reported.

evidence.title: Longitudinal profiles of the fecal metabolome during the first 2 years of life
evidence.study_population: 101 Latino infants, fecal metabolome at 1, 6, 12, 18 and 24 months
evidence.relevance: Most directly age-matched design found (includes 6- and 12-month timepoints), but the searchable content describes highly personalized, largely conserved profiles and does not report leukotriene F4 as an age-discriminating metabolite; treated as absence of specific support rather than contradiction.

evidence.title: Leukotriene F4 | CAS NO.:83851-42-7
evidence.relevance: States that LTF4 is a cysteinyl-leukotriene produced in vitro from LTE4 and not reported to date in vivo - an important caveat about whether an untargeted LC-MS feature annotated as LTF4 reflects a genuine endogenous compound in infant stool.

caveats: Two major caveats. (1) Annotation confidence: the feature is an ESI m/z-based lipidomics annotation, and multiple authoritative chemical sources state LTF4 has been produced in vitro (LTE4 + gamma-glutamyl transferase) but not demonstrated in vivo; isobaric/isomeric cysteinyl-leukotrienes and other glutathione-conjugated lipids could produce the same feature, so orthogonal confirmation (MS/MS, authentic standard) is advisable before interpreting biologically. (2) Direction ambiguity: plausible mechanisms exist in both directions - greater milk-derived ARA/eicosanoid input at 5 months versus greater microbial and dietary-lipid diversity plus more mature mucosal immune activity at 12 months - so the pathway-level reasoning alone should not be treated as supporting the hypothesis. Any signal in your data would essentially be a novel, unreplicated observation.
